title: The Character Table of $S_5$
---

The group $S_5$ has seven conjugacy classes, one for each cycle type:

<div class="table-wrap"><table class="tex-table has-stub"><tbody><tr><th scope="row" class="c">cycle type</th><td class="c">$1^5$</td><td class="c">$2 \cdot 1^3$</td><td class="c">$2^2 \cdot 1$</td><td class="c">$3 \cdot 1^2$</td><td class="c">$3 \cdot 2$</td><td class="c">$4 \cdot 1$</td><td class="c">$5$</td></tr><tr><th scope="row" class="c">representative</th><td class="c">$e$</td><td class="c">$(12)$</td><td class="c">$(12)(34)$</td><td class="c">$(123)$</td><td class="c">$(123)(45)$</td><td class="c">$(1234)$</td><td class="c">$(12345)$</td></tr><tr><th scope="row" class="c">size</th><td class="c">1</td><td class="c">10</td><td class="c">15</td><td class="c">20</td><td class="c">20</td><td class="c">30</td><td class="c">24</td></tr></tbody></table></div>

So it has seven irreducible representations, and the squares of their dimensions add up to $120$. We start from the ones we know.

- $U$ and $U'$, the only $1$-dimensional representations.
- The standard representation $V$, of dimension $4$, with $\chi_V = (4, 2, 0, 1, -1, 0, -1)$. It is irreducible, since $$H(\chi_V, \chi_V) = \tfrac{1}{120}\bigl(16 + 10 \cdot 4 + 0 + 20 \cdot 1 + 20 \cdot 1 + 0 + 24 \cdot 1\bigr) = 1.$$
- The twist $V' = V \otimes U'$, irreducible of dimension $4$, with $\chi_{V'} = \chi_V\sgn = (4, -2, 0, 1, 1, 0, -1)$. It is not isomorphic to $V$, since the characters differ at $(12)$.

These account for $1 + 1 + 16 + 16 = 34$, so the remaining three irreducible representations have dimensions $d_1 \leq d_2 \leq d_3$ with $d_1^2 + d_2^2 + d_3^2 = 86$, and $d_1 \geq 2$ because $U$ and $U'$ are the only $1$-dimensional ones. Then $3d_3^2 \geq 86$ and $d_3^2 \leq 86 - 8$, so $d_3 \in \{6, 7, 8\}$; this leaves $22$, $37$ or $50$ for $d_1^2 + d_2^2$, and the only way to write one of these as a sum of two squares of integers $\geq 2$ is $50 = 5^2 + 5^2$. So the remaining dimensions are $5$, $5$ and $6$.

## <span class="num">14.3.1</span> Finding the Remaining Irreducibles

The most effective way to find them is to decompose $V \otimes V$, of dimension $16$, or rather its two pieces $\Sym^2 V$ and $\bigwedge^2 V$, of dimensions $10$ and $6$. By Proposition [13.4.3](/notes/math-55a/13-4-characters#proposition-13-4-3)(vi), $$\chi_{\Sym^2 V}(g) = \tfrac12\bigl(\chi_V(g)^2 + \chi_V(g^2)\bigr), \qquad \chi_{\bigwedge^2 V}(g) = \tfrac12\bigl(\chi_V(g)^2 - \chi_V(g^2)\bigr),$$ which come from the fact that if $g$ has eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_4$ on $V$, then it has eigenvalues $\lambda_i\lambda_j$, $i \leq j$, on $\Sym^2 V$ and $\lambda_i\lambda_j$, $i < j$, on $\bigwedge^2 V$. To use them we need $\chi_V(g^2)$. Squaring the representatives: $(12)^2 = ((12)(34))^2 = e$; $(123)^2 = (132)$ and $((123)(45))^2 = (132)$ are $3$-cycles; $(1234)^2 = (13)(24)$ is a double transposition; and $(12345)^2 = (13524)$ is a $5$-cycle. This gives:

<div class="table-wrap"><table class="tex-table has-stub"><thead><tr><th scope="col" class="c"></th><th scope="col" class="c">$e$</th><th scope="col" class="c">$(12)$</th><th scope="col" class="c">$(12)(34)$</th><th scope="col" class="c">$(123)$</th><th scope="col" class="c">$(123)(45)$</th><th scope="col" class="c">$(1234)$</th><th scope="col" class="c">$(12345)$</th></tr><tr><th scope="col" class="c">size</th><th scope="col" class="c">1</th><th scope="col" class="c">10</th><th scope="col" class="c">15</th><th scope="col" class="c">20</th><th scope="col" class="c">20</th><th scope="col" class="c">30</th><th scope="col" class="c">24</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row" class="c">$\chi_V(g)$</th><td class="c">4</td><td class="c">2</td><td class="c">0</td><td class="c">1</td><td class="c">$-1$</td><td class="c">0</td><td class="c">$-1$</td></tr><tr><th scope="row" class="c">$\chi_V(g^2)$</th><td class="c">4</td><td class="c">4</td><td class="c">4</td><td class="c">1</td><td class="c">1</td><td class="c">0</td><td class="c">$-1$</td></tr><tr><th scope="row" class="c">$\chi_{\bigwedge^2 V}$</th><td class="c">6</td><td class="c">0</td><td class="c">$-2$</td><td class="c">0</td><td class="c">0</td><td class="c">0</td><td class="c">1</td></tr><tr><th scope="row" class="c">$\chi_{\Sym^2 V}$</th><td class="c">10</td><td class="c">4</td><td class="c">2</td><td class="c">1</td><td class="c">1</td><td class="c">0</td><td class="c">0</td></tr></tbody></table></div>

First, $\bigwedge^2 V$ is irreducible: $$H(\chi_{\bigwedge^2 V}, \chi_{\bigwedge^2 V}) = \tfrac{1}{120}\bigl(36 + 0 + 15 \cdot 4 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 24 \cdot 1\bigr) = \tfrac{120}{120} = 1.$$ It is the $6$-dimensional irreducible representation. Next, $$H(\chi_{\Sym^2 V}, \chi_{\Sym^2 V}) = \tfrac{1}{120}\bigl(100 + 10 \cdot 16 + 15 \cdot 4 + 20 \cdot 1 + 20 \cdot 1 + 0 + 0\bigr) = \tfrac{360}{120} = 3,$$ so $\Sym^2 V$ is a direct sum of three pairwise non-isomorphic irreducible representations. Two of them are $U$ and $V$: $$\begin{aligned}
H(\chi_U, \chi_{\Sym^2 V}) &= \tfrac{1}{120}(10 + 40 + 30 + 20 + 20 + 0 + 0) = 1, \\
H(\chi_V, \chi_{\Sym^2 V}) &= \tfrac{1}{120}(40 + 80 + 0 + 20 - 20 + 0 + 0) = 1.
\end{aligned}$$ So $\Sym^2 V \cong U \oplus V \oplus W$, where $W$ is irreducible of dimension $10 - 1 - 4 = 5$, with character $$\chi_W = \chi_{\Sym^2 V} - \chi_U - \chi_V = (5, 1, 1, -1, 1, -1, 0).$$ Finally, $W' = W \otimes U'$ is irreducible with character $\chi_W\sgn = (5, -1, 1, -1, -1, 1, 0)$, and $W' \not\cong W$ because the characters differ at $(12)$. This gives all seven irreducible representations.

class="c">$-2$</td><td class="c">0</td><td class="c">0</td><td class="c">0</td><td class="c">1</td></tr></tbody></table></div>

As checks, $1 + 1 + 16 + 16 + 25 + 25 + 36 = 120$, and column orthogonality holds; for instance, the column of $(12)$ gives $1 + 1 + 4 + 4 + 1 + 1 + 0 = 12 = 120/10$.

:::note
The exterior powers $\bigwedge^k V$ of the standard representation of $S_5$ are $\bigwedge^0 V = U$, $\bigwedge^1 V = V$, the irreducible $\bigwedge^2 V$, $\bigwedge^3 V \cong V'$ and $\bigwedge^4 V \cong U'$ (see the exercises), so all of them are irreducible. This is a general fact: for the standard representation $V$ of $S_n$, every $\bigwedge^k V$ with $0 \leq k \leq n - 1$ is irreducible (Fulton and Harris, *Representation Theory: A First Course*, §3.2).
:::
